answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1925–1965 · Minister, Black nationalist leader & founder of the Organization of Afro-American Unity
answer.sourceLine: Malcolm X said it at an Organization of Afro-American Unity rally in the Audubon Ballroom, Harlem, on 13 December 1964, while setting up a passage about how the American press covered the Congo. The sentence was printed the following year in Malcolm X Speaks, the collection George Breitman assembled after the assassination, and the circulating wording matches the published transcript almost exactly.

source.heading: The speech

docMeta.dd: 13 December 1964 — OAAU rally, Audubon Ballroom, Harlem, New York
Malcolm X Speaks: Selected Speeches and Statements (Merit Publishers, 1965), ed. George Breitman

source.excerpt: The press is so powerful in its image-making role, it can make a criminal look like he’s the victim and make the victim look like he’s the criminal. … If you aren’t careful, the newspapers will have you hating the people who are being oppressed and loving the people who are doing the oppressing.
trail: Started with the specialists. Quote Investigator has not taken this one up, so the anchor is Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗, which gives a speech at the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem on 13 December 1964, published in Malcolm X Speaks (1965), ed. George Breitman, p. 93.

Checked that against a transcript rather than another quote page. The Missouri S&T–hosted Collected Speeches, Debates & Interviews (1960–1965) ↗ carries the whole speech under the heading “At the Audubon Ballroom (December 13, 1964)”, and the sentence is there word for word on p. 276, inside the Congo passage.

Confirmed the occasion independently: Abdul Alkalimat’s Malcolm X audio archive ↗ logs a ~70-minute recording of the 13 December 1964 OAAU rally at the Audubon, with Dick Gregory and Babu also speaking.
Ruled out the neighbouring speech. The Audubon address of 20 December 1964, printed in the same book at pp. 115–136 and posted in full by Teaching American History ↗, does not contain the line.
source.excerptNote: Transcript wording. Note “If you aren’t careful” and no comma before “and loving” — the widely shared “If you’re not careful …, and loving …” is a smoothed version of this.

author.name: Malcolm X
author.heading: About Malcolm X
author.metaLine: 1925–1965 · American minister, Black nationalist leader & founder of the Organization of Afro-American Unity
author.bio: Born Malcolm Little in Omaha, Nebraska on 19 May 1925, he became the Nation of Islam’s most visible minister and national spokesman before publicly breaking with the organisation in March 1964. In the last year of his life he made the hajj, took the name El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz, and founded the secular, Pan-Africanist Organization of Afro-American Unity, whose Harlem rallies gave him a platform independent of the Nation. He was assassinated on 21 February 1965 — on the stage of the same Audubon Ballroom where he spoke these words ten weeks earlier.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake. It is one of the better-documented lines in the Malcolm X corpus — you can name the hall, the date and the page. What goes wrong is everything around the sentence: it circulates with no source at all, its punctuation drifts, and there are two Audubon Ballroom speeches a week apart to confuse the citation.

items.why: BrainyQuote prints the sentence in exactly the published wording — and attaches no speech, no date and no book ↗, only his birth and death years. That is how a genuine, datable quote ends up looking like folklore.

items.who: The smoothed ‘If you’re not careful’ version
items.why: The most-shared form reads “If you’re not careful … being oppressed, and loving …” — that is how Goodreads’ community-added entry ↗ has it. The published transcript reads “If you aren’t careful … being oppressed and loving …”, without the comma. Same meaning, tidied speech.

Malcolm spoke at the Audubon again a week later, and it is that second speech — Malcolm X Speaks, pp. 115–136 — that is most widely reprinted online ↗. The newspaper line is not in it. It belongs to the 13 December rally.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Malcolm X’s own, spoken at an OAAU rally in the Audubon Ballroom on 13 December 1964 and printed the next year in Malcolm X Speaks — you can read the whole passage in the full transcript ↗.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: This was not abstract media theory. Malcolm was warming up an OAAU crowd waiting on a guest speaker, and the subject was the Congo — villages being bombed from American-supplied aircraft flown by anti-Castro Cuban pilots, while the story that gripped the American press was the fate of a few white hostages. The newspaper line is the hinge he swings into that argument: the coverage had inverted who was the criminal and who was the victim.

He then turned it inward, warning the room that the same inversion works on the reader — that a person can be talked into hating himself and admiring the man who is beating him. That is the part the quote’s modern circulation usually drops, and it is the reason the sentence is a warning about the audience rather than a complaint about journalists.
context.detailsSummary: How the sentence got into print
detailsBody: Malcolm X did not publish this himself. Malcolm X Speaks: Selected Speeches and Statements was edited by George Breitman, a socialist editor who had been transcribing and preserving the speeches, and it came out in 1965 from Merit Publishers — a small Trotskyist imprint later folded into Pathfinder Press — months after the assassination. Grove Press issued the paperback that keeps it in print today.

One trap for anyone chasing the citation: the book contains two Audubon Ballroom speeches from December 1964, a week apart. The newspaper passage is in the 13 December one. The 20 December speech, widely reprinted online, is a different text.
